title: Sri Lanka, Maldives, Myanmar and Impediments to Cooperation

cards.b:
Sri Lanka and the Maldives lie on the Indian Ocean sea lanes that carry most of India's trade and energy. Myanmar is India's land bridge to Southeast Asia. All three are courted by China.

These countries show the limits of Indian influence. India has large aid, culture and security ties with each, but each also shows that small states can bargain between big powers. Politics at home can flip a relationship overnight.

The syllabus title ends with "impediments to cooperation". Prepare a general list (asymmetry, trust deficit, China, domestic politics, delays) and then give country examples.

cards.h: Sri Lanka: from war to aid
cards.b:
The Indo-Lanka Accord (29 July 1987), signed by Rajiv Gandhi and J.R. Jayewardene, created Provincial Councils via Sri Lanka's 13th Amendment. The Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) went in, fought the LTTE and left in 1990 at heavy cost. Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated by the LTTE in 1991. J.N. Dixit's Assignment Colombo (1998) is the insider account.

After 2009, India pushed for Tamil rights and devolution and was criticised at the UNHRC for abstaining or voting inconsistently.

In the 2022 economic collapse India extended about $4 billion in credit lines, currency swaps and fuel support, and gave early financing assurances that helped Sri Lanka secure an IMF programme.

Anura Kumara Dissanayake (NPP, a leftist) won the presidency in September 2024. His first state visit abroad was to India (December 2024). Modi visited Colombo in April 2025 and signed a defence cooperation MoU, plus energy and connectivity deals (a Trincomalee energy hub, a land bridge idea, power grid links).

Colombo says its land and ports will not be used against India's security. It has paused visits by Chinese research vessels through a moratorium and rules, though Chinese projects such as the Colombo Port City and a Hambantota refinery continue.

Irritants: fishermen arrests in the Palk Strait, Katchatheevu (ceded in 1974 and 1976 agreements; revived as a political issue in Tamil Nadu), Tamil rights.

cards.h: The Maldives: from 'India Out' to a reset
cards.b:
India has been the Maldives' first responder: Operation Cactus (1988) stopped a coup, and India gave water and aid in crises.

  • 2023: Mohamed Muizzu won on an 'India Out' campaign. Roughly 80–90 Indian military personnel who ran India-gifted helicopters and a Dornier aircraft were replaced by civilians by May 2024.
  • January 2024: a social media spat after Maldivian ministers mocked Modi's Lakshadweep trip.
  • China: a free trade agreement (signed January 2024) and defence cooperation, plus research-vessel visits.
  • India's support: rupee-dirham swap and budget support in 2024 to avert default. Modi attended the 60th Independence anniversary in July 2025, offering a large line of credit and starting free trade talks.
  • Greater Malé Connectivity Project, built with Indian funds, is a flagship.

In late 2026 reports said Muizzu visited Pakistan and signed defence MoUs, which Delhi watched closely.

cards.h: Myanmar: India's gateway to the East
cards.b:
Myanmar matters for the Act East policy and the Northeast. Major projects:

  • Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project: sea from Kolkata to Sittwe, river to Paletwa, then road to Mizoram. Sittwe port operates; the road section is delayed by conflict.
  • India–Myanmar–Thailand Trilateral Highway (about 1,360 km, Moreh to Mae Sot), long delayed.

Since the coup of 1 February 2021, India has avoided isolating the junta, citing the need for border cooperation and a hedge against China. China's pipelines and its Kyaukpyu port are a rival presence. The Arakan Army controls much of Rakhine, near the Kaladan route.

India ended the Free Movement Regime (16 km visa-free zone) from 2024 and plans to fence the border, which angers Mizoram and Nagaland. A junta-run election was held in phases from December 2025; in April 2026 the new parliament elected Min Aung Hlaing president, after he gave up command of the army. India gave earthquake relief in March 2025 under Operation Brahma.

1. Asymmetry: India's size makes neighbours anxious.
  2. Trust deficit and India–Pakistan rivalry that freezes SAARC.
  3. China's inroads: loans, ports, arms.
  4. Domestic politics: 'India Out' campaigns, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal pressing the Centre on fisheries and water.
  5. Delays: Indian projects can be slow (Kaladan, the Trilateral Highway).
  6. Border issues: migration, smuggling, insurgents, refugees (Rohingya and Chin).
  7. Bilateral baggage: boundary and water disputes.
  8. Weak regional institutions and low intra-regional trade.

For each, add one example and one policy response. This makes answers specific.

cards.h: South Asia as a regional security complex
cards.b:
Barry Buzan and Ole Wæver (Regions and Powers, 2003) define a regional security complex: states whose security problems are so linked that they cannot be analysed apart. South Asia is a classic case, centred on the India–Pakistan rivalry.

Buzan notes India's problem: small neighbours see India as the threat, and India sees outside powers (China, the US) as threats. This makes India a regional hegemon that cannot fully act as one.

Two doctrines are often contrasted. The Indira Doctrine (a Monroe-like belief that no external power should intervene in the region) and the Gujral Doctrine (generosity without reciprocity). Modi's Neighbourhood First combines delivery with a firm line on security.

India's best argument is geography: it cannot move away from its neighbours, and a stable neighbourhood is in India's interest. Its weakness is execution: late projects and uneven treatment.

The 2024–26 pattern shows neighbours do not choose between India and China. They take from both. India's task is to be the more reliable and quicker of the two.

• Crisis aid first (Sri Lanka 2022, Maldives swaps, Myanmar quake 2025).
  • Security presence: the Colombo Security Conclave, coastal radar networks, hydrography help.
  • Connectivity with local ownership: Malé bridge, Sri Lanka's energy links, Sittwe port.
  • Digital public infrastructure: UPI in Sri Lanka and the Maldives (RuPay too).
  • Soft power: Buddhism, scholarships, ITEC training.

Always link to SAGAR/MAHASAGAR and the Indian Ocean Region. Add that India is the first responder across the region.

"India has been losing ground in its neighbourhood. Critically comment." (typical)
"Examine the impediments to regional cooperation in South Asia, with examples." (typical)
"Discuss India's strategic interests in Sri Lanka and the Maldives." (typical)

Structure: (1) context: Indian Ocean and Act East; (2) country by country: Sri Lanka, Maldives, Myanmar; (3) China factor; (4) the checklist of impediments; (5) India's responses; (6) way forward: faster delivery, consult, balance.

quiz.q: The Indo-Lanka Accord was signed in:
quiz.w: 29 July 1987 by Rajiv Gandhi and J.R. Jayewardene.

quiz.q: The 13th Amendment of Sri Lanka's Constitution relates to:
quiz.w: It created Provincial Councils, flowing from the 1987 Accord.

quiz.q: Operation Cactus (1988) took place in the:
quiz.w: India helped foil a coup against President Gayoom.

quiz.q: Katchatheevu island was ceded to Sri Lanka by agreements of:
quiz.w: The Indira Gandhi–Bandaranaike agreements of 1974 and 1976.

quiz.q: Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project links Kolkata to:
quiz.w: Kolkata–Sittwe by sea, then Kaladan river and road to Mizoram.

quiz.q: Who won Sri Lanka's presidency in September 2024?
The Maldives president elected in 2023 on an 'India Out' platform was:
Buzan and Wæver's 'regional security complex' theory appears in:
quiz.w: Regions and Powers: The Structure of International Security (2003).

quiz.q: Which agreement does India's Free Movement Regime refer to?
o: Visa-free 16 km zone on the Myanmar border
quiz.w: The FMR allowed visa-free movement within 16 km; India moved to end it in 2024.

quiz.q: The Greater Malé Connectivity Project is funded mainly by:
quiz.w: It is India-funded, with grants and lines of credit.
